_note: The Turn — reduction to a claim. The DOORS are attested reading-traditions surfaced from the retrieved reception store (~/reception-corpus), NOT authored from recall; every witness `reading` is the source's own words, lightly trimmed (Glossa editorial source-markers like ((HIER.)) and ((BEDA.)) dropped; the Migne recension's own 'etc., as far as' abridgements are marked with '...'). The editorial framing (trap/hinge/gravity/synthesis/claim/say/do/subtract) is AI-drafted and pending Wilson's curation. [Authored 2026-10-06, Opus, Phase 4b brief, born v2: the build carries one track ('single'). The store has NO Catena Aurea Fathers on Mark 1:1-8 (Calvin and Matthew Henry are index-only rows; Barnes and JFB not used), so the Gospel doors rest on the Glossa ordinaria (Migne) 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:5, 1:7 and 1:8, Wesley's Notes 1:4 and 1:7, and the Catena intertext notes on Mark 1 (Isaiah 40:3, Isaiah 40:9, Malachi 3:1, 2 Kings 1:8). Wesley's 1:1-1:2 rows are his outline of the whole Gospel, not notes on the verses, and were left aside; 1:3 is a bare cross-reference. Isaiah 40 doors from Glossa 40:1, 40:6, 40:8, 40:11, Wesley 40:2, 40:6, 40:9, 40:10, and Catena intertext notes (taken up at 2 Corinthians 1:3-7, 1 Peter 1:22-25, Luke 15:3-7); the Barth CD row on Isaiah 40:1-11 is an empty pointer and was not used. Psalm 85 rows (Glossa 85:8, 85:13; Wesley 85:9, 85:10, 85:13) inform gravity/synthesis only. Not used on the Gospel: the Glossa's Rebecca-and-Isaac bridal typology (1:4-1:5) and the levirate reading of the sandal (1:7, beyond the 'not the bridegroom' line).]
trap: John becomes a costume and a mood: camel hair, locusts, a wild man shouting, and a sermon that either scolds the congregation for not being ready for Christmas or turns repentance into a December self-improvement plan. Or the preacher skips John altogether and goes straight to the baby, so that the wilderness, the confession and the river never happen.
hinge: Mark calls it "the beginning of the good news" and then gives us not Jesus but a man in the desert telling people to confess their sins. The good news begins with a summons to repent, and the herald's whole message is that he is not the point. The preacher cannot make John the hero, and cannot skip him either.

doors.landing: The road God comes down by
doors.claim: Repentance is not a hurdle we clear before God will come. It is the road itself, the way by which God comes down to us and we go up to him, and it is made in the desert, where we fell.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: The way of the Lord by which he enters in unto men is penance, through which God comes down to us, and we ascend to him. Whence the angels are remembered as ascending and descending upon the Son of man.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: In the desert the voice and the cry are made: because the house of Judaea is deserted, standing empty and swept, without the Spirit of God, without prophet, king, priest. Whence Jesus and John seek what was lost in the desert. Where the devil conquered, there he is conquered: where man fell, there he rises again.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Preaching the baptism of repentance — That is, preaching repentance, and baptizing as a sign and means of it.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make ready the way of the Lord' quotes Isaiah 40:3 (LXX). The wilderness/way motif structures the whole prologue (John baptizes 'in the wilderness,' 1:4). (Quotation of Isaiah 40:3)

doors.say: Repentance isn't the toll you pay before God will come. It's the road he comes down on, and it runs through the very desert where you got lost.
doors.do: Invite them to name one wilderness place in their life, where they fell or went empty, and to make it this week's place of confession rather than the place they avoid.

doors.claim: The greatest prophet's whole message is that he is not the point. John will not even claim the slave's task of untying the sandal, because the one coming is mightier, and he baptizes not with water but with the Spirit.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose — That is, to do him the very meanest service.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Mightier than I. Who is mightier than the grace by which sins are washed away? ... I am not able to bare the feet of the Redeemer, because I claim not for myself the name of bridegroom.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: I have baptized you with water. John does not yet say openly that he is God or the Son of God, because his hearers were untaught: but little by little, through the humanity glorified, he leads them to faith in the divinity, saying: But he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: Mark's 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way' is a near-verbatim citation of Malachi 3:1. Coherence is total: the messenger prepares the way of the Lord. (Quotation of Malachi 3:1)

doors.say: John had crowds from the whole countryside, and he spent them all pointing past himself. The best thing a messenger can say is: not me, him.
doors.do: Ask them to look at one place they are a 'voice' (a family, a class, a team, this church) and to do one thing this week that points people past themselves to Christ.

doors.claim: Mark's gospel does not start with something new. It starts with what the prophets foretold, so that the good news of the Son of God arrives as an old promise finally beginning to be kept.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: The beginning of the Gospel. The Gospel, good tidings, which belongs properly to the kingdom of God and to the remission of sins. Whence: Repent ye and believe the Gospel: and the kingdom of heaven hath drawn nigh.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: As it is written. Mark sets the testimonies of the prophets first, by which he asserts that these things are old and not new, but foreknown and foretold by the prophets, and in this he invites also the Jews, who had received the law and the prophets, to the Gospel.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: Isaiah 40:9 pairs 'good tidings' with Zion's herald immediately before the 40:3 'voice in the wilderness' that Mark quotes in 1:3. The proximity of the two Isaiah loci makes it likely Mark heard 'gospel' from this same context. (Echo of Isaiah 40:9, contested)

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: John's garb of camel's hair and a leather belt around the waist deliberately mirrors Elijah, 'a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist.' Coherence is strong: John is the returning Elijah of Malachi. (Allusion of 2 Kings 1:8)

doors.say: The good news doesn't start in Bethlehem. It starts in Isaiah, and in Malachi, and in Elijah's belt: God beginning, at last, to keep what he promised long ago.
doors.do: Have them find one promise of God they were taught long ago and have quietly stopped expecting, and pray it this week as though it had just begun to come true.

doors.claim: God's first word to an exhausted people is not a command but comfort, spoken to the heart, and its cause is that the sin is forgiven and the hard service is over.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Speak ye to the heart. He speaks to the heart who comforts one that is sorrowful, as it is said of Sichem: Sichem spoke to her heart, and comforted her. ... It is forgiven. The cause of consolation, the remission of sins.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Warfare — The time of her captivity, and misery. Double - Not twice as much as her sins deserved, but abundantly enough to answer God's design in this chastisement, which was to humble and reform them, and to warn others by their example.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: The titulature 'God of all comfort' who 'comforts us in all our affliction' draws directly on the programmatic 'Comfort, comfort my people' that opens Second Isaiah. (taken up at 2 Corinthians 1:3-7)

doors.say: Before God tells his people to do anything, he tells his preachers to speak to their hearts: the sentence is served, the sin is pardoned.
doors.do: Ask them to bring one word of comfort to someone whose 'warfare' has gone on too long, and to say it to the heart, not just to the situation.

doors.landing: The grass withers; the word stands
doors.claim: The prophet hesitates to preach to a people who wither like grass. The answer is not that they are sturdier than they look but that the word of God is, and what God has spoken will be done.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: What shall I cry? Not without cause does he ask: for when he had offered himself of his own accord, saying: Behold I, send me: he announced hard things to his own people, and now he fears the same.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: All that men are or have, yea, their highest accomplishments, are but like the grass of the field, weak and vanishing, soon nipt and brought to nothing; but God's word is like himself, immutable and irresistible: and therefore as the mouth of the Lord, and not of man, hath spoken these things, so doubt not but they shall be fulfilled.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: But the word of the Lord. The Word is Christ with his body, which is the Church.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: Verbatim, formula-introduced citation ('For, All flesh is like grass... the grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of the Lord endures forever'). Peter quotes the LXX of Isaiah 40:6-8 to ground the imperishable seed/word. (taken up at 1 Peter 1:22-25)

doors.say: You are grass, and so is everything you are proud of. That is not the bad news. The good news is that God's word does not wither, and it has been spoken over you.
doors.do: Invite them to name one accomplishment or security they lean on that will fade, and to memorise Isaiah 40:8 to set against it this week.

doors.landing: Behold your God: arm and bosom
doors.claim: The herald is sent up the mountain to say one thing, "Behold your God," and the God who comes is both strong enough to need no help and tender enough to carry the lambs.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Get up - That thy voice may be better heard. Afraid - Lest thou shouldest be found a false prophet. Behold - Take notice of this wonderful work, and glorious appearance of your God.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: His arm — He shall need no succors, for his own power shall be sufficient to govern his people, and to destroy his adversaries.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: His flock. Now by contemplation, in the time to come by vision itself: now by teaching, afterward by saving or by satisfying. Them that are with young. Teachers daily bringing forth sons to God.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: The shepherd who gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom illuminates the man carrying the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing. The tender carrying gesture is distinctive and shared, strengthening the divine-shepherd reading. (taken up at Luke 15:3-7)

doors.say: The God who is coming doesn't need your help to win, and he isn't too strong to stoop. He carries the lambs and leads gently those who are struggling.
doors.do: Have them name someone in the congregation who is 'with young' (carrying a heavy load of care) and find one way to carry part of it with them this week.

single.gravity: Advent's second week opens with comfort and a road. Isaiah is told to speak to Jerusalem's heart: her hard service is over, her sin is pardoned; a voice cries to make a highway in the desert; all flesh is grass but the word of God stands; and the Lord comes with a strong arm and carries the lambs (Isaiah 40). The Psalm hears God speak peace and sees mercy and truth meet, righteousness going before him to make a path for his steps (Psalm 85). Peter says the Lord is not slow but patient, not wanting any to perish, and asks what kind of people we ought to be as we wait. Mark opens with Isaiah's voice in the wilderness and a crowd confessing its sins in the Jordan. The nerve: the comfort comes down the same road as the call to repent.

synthesis.convergence: Isaiah's comfort is that sin is forgiven and God is coming, so prepare his way in the desert (Isaiah 40). The Psalm promises that righteousness will go before him and make a path for his feet (Psalm 85). Peter reads the delay as patience that leads to repentance (2 Peter 3). Mark sends John into that very desert, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins and pointing past himself to the one who will baptize with the Spirit (Mark 1). Every reading puts a road between our wilderness and God's arrival, and the road is repentance received as comfort.
synthesis.claim: God's comfort and God's call to repent are one word: the sin is pardoned, so make the road straight, because he is coming to carry you.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that hears 'repent' as scolding and 'comfort' as a holiday mood, the move is to put them back together: repentance is the comfort of being met in the desert, and the one who comes is the shepherd who carries the lambs.

subtract: These three are doors, not points. Each is a different landing: repentance as the road God comes down by, the herald who points past himself, and the good news as an old promise beginning. Walk through one and let the other two go; the choosing is the sermon's focus.
source: Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and Catena intertextual notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus. Attested, not authored. (No Catena Aurea Fathers are on file for Mark.)
